buildUp: To show depth, each eye needs its own image, so there are two displays, one per eye, each drawn from that eye's position.

The screens are only a few centimetres from your eyes, too close to focus on, so a lens in front of each one makes the picture look large and far away, and a wheel slides them to match the spacing of your eyes.
Ordinary lenses need a long gap to the screen, which would make the visor stick far out from your face; folded pancake lenses shrink that gap, at the cost of needing very bright screens.

To keep the world still, the headset must know where your head is at every moment, so motion sensors inside and wide-angle cameras outside track it, and the same cameras follow your hands and controllers.
Drawing two high-resolution images 90 or more times a second takes a powerful chip, which needs a fan and a battery, all carried on your head.

Finally comfort and the real world: colour cameras and a depth sensor let you see the room through the headset, and a face cushion, strap and side-firing speakers spread the weight of about half a kilogram and leave your ears uncovered.
firstPrinciples.coreIdea: Give each eye its own small screen showing the scene from that eye's viewpoint, use lenses to make the screens look large and far away, and redraw both images so quickly after every head movement that the virtual world seems to stay still. Cameras on the front and motion sensors inside keep track of exactly where your head is, so the headset always knows what each eye should be seeing.

hardParts.title: Keeping the virtual world nailed in place
hardParts.why: Tracking has to find your head's position to within millimetres, many times a second, using only cameras looking at an unknown room and sensors that drift. Then the chip must draw two images and get them onto the screens within about 20 milliseconds of you moving, or the world wobbles and people feel ill.

hardParts.title: Optics that are wide, sharp and thin
hardParts.why: The lenses must cover a field of view of about 110 degrees, stay sharp across it, and sit only a couple of centimetres from the screen. Pancake lenses achieve the thin part by folding light, but they throw away most of it, so the displays must be very bright and very dense, packing over 1,200 pixels into each inch.

hardParts.title: Seeing the real room through cameras
hardParts.why: The colour cameras sit a few centimetres in front of your eyes, so their raw view would make objects look closer and in the wrong place. The chip uses depth information to warp every frame to where your eyes would really see things, with only a few tens of milliseconds of delay, so you can reach out and pick up a real cup.

principles.explanation: Your brain judges depth from the slightly different views of your two eyes, so a headset draws the scene twice, once from each eye's position. Your eyes are about 63 mm apart, so each sees a nearby object from a slightly different angle. Your brain measures that difference and turns it into a feeling of depth; hold up a finger and close each eye in turn to see it jump. The two virtual cameras sit the same distance apart as your eyes, and the spacing wheel moves the lenses so their centres line up with your pupils.
principles.title: Two eyes, two viewpoints, one sense of depth

principles.explanation: The screens sit just a few centimetres away, too close for your eyes to focus on, so a lens in front of each makes them look large and about a metre or two off. Put a screen just inside the focal length of a lens and the lens makes an enlarged image that appears much farther off, exactly like a magnifying glass over small print. A pancake lens folds the light back and forth between partly reflecting layers so it can sit very close to the screen, but each bounce loses light, so at most about a quarter gets through.
principles.title: A magnifying glass for each eye

principles.explanation: If the picture lags behind your head even slightly, your eyes and inner ear disagree and you can feel sick, so the image must follow every movement within about 20 milliseconds. The balance organs in your inner ear feel every turn of your head, and your brain expects your eyes to agree. If the image lags, the world seems to slosh as you move, and that mismatch is a classic cause of motion sickness. Turn your head at 100 degrees a second and even a 20 millisecond delay lets the world slip 2 degrees, about 50 pixels at roughly 25 pixels per degree.
principles.title: Your inner ear checks the picture

principles.explanation: Combining fast motion sensors that drift with slower cameras that don't gives tracking that is both fast and steady, like a walker counting steps but checking landmarks. Motion sensors measure turning and acceleration up to about 1,000 times a second, but working out position from them means adding up many small readings, and their small errors add up too, so the estimate drifts. Cameras are slower but see fixed features in the room, like the corner of a table, which pins the estimate back in place.
principles.title: Fast sensors that drift, slow cameras that don't

firstPrinciples.problem: Convince your brain that you're standing somewhere else. The picture has to fill your vision, have real depth, and stay perfectly fixed in space as you turn your head, or you feel sick; and all of it has to be worn on your face. Sharper, faster images need more computing, which means more power, more heat and more weight hanging off the front of your head.

questions.answer: Your eyes can't focus that close, so it would just be a blur. The headset's lenses make the screens appear about a metre or two away, where your eyes can focus comfortably.
questions.question: Why can't you get the same effect by holding a phone screen a few centimetres from your eyes?

questions.answer: With a TV, your head isn't driving the picture, so nothing disagrees. In a headset your inner ear feels your head turn, and if the image lags behind, your eyes and balance sense contradict each other.
questions.question: Why can a laggy headset make you feel sick when a laggy video game on a TV doesn't?

questions.answer: Each lens is only sharp near its centre, so if your pupils sit off-centre the picture blurs and can look slightly distorted. Depth can also feel a little wrong, because the headset assumes your eyes are where the lenses are.
questions.question: What goes wrong if the lens spacing doesn't match the distance between your eyes?

firstPrinciples.xFactor: Fooling the brain depends more on timing than on pixels: a slightly soft picture that keeps up with your head feels real, while a sharp one that lags makes you queasy. So headsets predict where your head is about to be, draw for that moment, and then shift the finished image once more using the very latest sensor reading just before it reaches the screen. That last-moment correction hides much of the delay that would otherwise give the illusion away.

name: VR Headset
overview:
A VR headset puts a separate screen in front of each eye, each showing the scene from a slightly different viewpoint, so your brain fuses the two into one 3D world. Lenses between your eyes and the screens make the small panels fill most of your vision and let your eyes focus as if the image were a metre or two away rather than a few centimetres.

The hard part is keeping the picture locked to the world as you move. Cameras on the outside of the visor watch the room many times a second, and motion sensors inside measure every tilt and turn; the chip combines the two to work out exactly where your head is and redraws both screens fast enough, typically 90 or more times a second, that the world seems to stay still. The same cameras find your hands and controllers, and colour cameras let the headset show you the real room with virtual objects mixed in.

A standalone headset carries everything with it: a phone-class chip with a small fan, a battery for a couple of hours of play, speakers aimed at your ears from the side straps, and a soft face cushion and strap that spread the weight of about half a kilogram across your face and head.

parts.description: Glossy front panel with windows for the cameras and depth sensor; it's where your hand taps to toggle passthrough.

details.didYouKnow: Many plastics that look completely black are almost clear to infrared light, which is why tracking cameras and infrared sensors can hide behind what looks like a solid dark panel.
details.howItWorks: The front cover protects the cameras and sensors while letting them see out through small windows. The tap gesture does not use a button at all: the motion sensors on the logic board feel the tiny jolt when your fingers knock on the cover, and software recognises the pattern. Behind it, the cover also helps channel air towards the vents so the fan can do its job.
keyNumbers: Roughly 18 to 19 cm wide
Typically about 5 camera and sensor windows
Usually a double tap to switch passthrough on or off
details.madeOf: Injection-moulded plastic such as polycarbonate, often with a glossy coating. Some of the camera windows are made from dark plastic that looks black to us but lets infrared light straight through.

parts.name: Front cover

parts.description: Colour camera roughly in line with your left eye that films the room so you can see it through the headset.

details.didYouKnow: Mixed reality only feels comfortable if the passthrough delay is tiny; if the real world lags behind your head movement, the mismatch between what your eyes and inner ears report can make you feel queasy.
details.howItWorks: This camera records the room in colour so the headset can show it on the left display, letting you see your surroundings without taking the headset off. Because it sits a few centimetres in front of your actual eye, the chip uses depth information to warp each frame so that objects appear where your left eye would really see them. Virtual objects are then drawn on top, which is what makes mixed reality possible.
keyNumbers: Roughly 4 MP resolution
Delay from capture to display typically a few tens of milliseconds
Sits roughly 3 cm off-centre, in line with the left eye
details.madeOf: A small stack of moulded plastic or glass lenses over a silicon colour image sensor, much like a phone camera. A cover window of glass or clear plastic in the front cover keeps dust and fingerprints off the lens itself.

parts.name: Left colour passthrough camera

parts.description: Wide-angle black-and-white camera that maps the room and follows your hands and controllers.

details.didYouKnow: This approach, called inside-out tracking, uses a technique known as SLAM, short for simultaneous localisation and mapping, which robots and self-driving cars also use to find their way around.
details.howItWorks: This camera watches the left side and lower front of the room, picking out corners, edges and textures it can recognise from frame to frame. By seeing how those features shift as you move, and combining that with the motion sensors, the chip works out where your head is without any external base stations. It also sees infrared lights hidden in the controllers and the shapes of your fingers for hand tracking.
keyNumbers: Field of view typically well over 100 degrees
Resolution typically well under 1 MP
Usually one of about four tracking cameras
details.madeOf: A wide-angle lens over a black-and-white sensor that is sensitive to infrared as well as visible light. Black-and-white sensors collect more light per pixel than colour ones, which helps in dim rooms.

parts.name: Left tracking camera

parts.description: Colour camera roughly in line with your right eye that films the room so you can see it through the headset.

details.didYouKnow: Passthrough text is often harder to read than the real thing because the cameras capture fewer pixels per degree than your eyes can resolve, so small print on a phone screen can look slightly soft.
details.howItWorks: The right colour camera works as a pair with the left one, so the headset has two slightly different views of the room, just as your eyes do. That gives passthrough a natural sense of depth, so you can judge how far away a table or a doorway is. Its image is warped to match your right eye's position and fed to the right display many times a second.
keyNumbers: Roughly 4 MP resolution
Typically refreshed around 90 times a second to match the displays
Roughly 6 cm apart from the left camera
details.madeOf: Plastic or glass lens elements in a tiny barrel over a colour image sensor, with an infrared-cut filter so the colours look natural. It is the same kind of camera module found on the back of many smartphones.

parts.name: Right colour passthrough camera

parts.description: Wide-angle black-and-white camera that maps the room and follows your hands and controllers.

details.didYouKnow: Inside-out tracking can struggle with plain white walls, large mirrors and very dark rooms, because the cameras need visible texture to recognise where they are.
details.howItWorks: Mounted on the right corner and angled outwards, this camera covers the part of the room your right hand and controller usually move through. Its view overlaps with the other tracking cameras so a feature seen by two cameras at once can be located in 3D. If you raise a controller out of view of all the cameras, the headset falls back on the controller's own motion sensors for a moment.
keyNumbers: Typically tens of frames per second
Field of view typically well over 100 degrees
Sits roughly 7 cm right of centre
details.madeOf: A fisheye-style wide-angle lens over a monochrome sensor with a global shutter, which captures every pixel at the same instant. That avoids the bending and smearing a phone camera shows when things move quickly.

parts.name: Right tracking camera

parts.description: Infrared projector and sensor that measure distance to walls and furniture, so virtual things sit on real surfaces.

details.didYouKnow: Similar infrared depth sensing was popularised by a living-room gaming camera in 2010, and the same idea now unlocks phones with your face.
details.howItWorks: The sensor sends out invisible infrared light and measures how it comes back from surfaces, giving a distance for many points in the room at once. The headset combines those readings into a 3D mesh of walls, floor and furniture, so a virtual ball can bounce off your real sofa or a virtual window can sit flat on a real wall. It also helps the passthrough cameras get depth right when warping their images.
keyNumbers: Typically measures distances up to a few metres
Uses infrared light with wavelengths just under 1 micrometre
Room scan usually takes about a minute or less
details.madeOf: An infrared emitter and an infrared-sensitive receiver behind a window that blocks visible light but passes infrared. The emitter is usually a small laser or LED chip mounted on the same module as the receiver.

parts.name: Depth sensor

parts.description: Circuit board standing up behind the front cover, carrying the chip, memory, storage, Wi-Fi and motion sensors.

details.didYouKnow: Wi-Fi 6E's extra 6 GHz band is often much less crowded than older bands, which helps when streaming games wirelessly from a PC, where every millisecond of delay counts.
details.howItWorks: The board connects the processor to its memory and storage, the cameras, the displays, the speakers and the battery. It also carries the motion sensors, an accelerometer and gyroscope that report your head's movement hundreds of times a second, far faster than the cameras, so the headset can predict exactly where you will be looking when the next frame appears. A Wi-Fi radio lets you download games or stream from a PC.
keyNumbers: About 8 GB of memory
Typically 128 to 512 GB of storage
Motion sensors read up to about 1,000 times a second
Wi-Fi 6E uses the 6 GHz band
details.madeOf: A many-layered fibreglass and epoxy board with fine copper tracks between the layers. Packing wiring into stacked layers lets a board this small connect hundreds of chip pins.

parts.name: Logic board

parts.description: Phone-class system-on-chip that tracks your head and hands and draws two images at once, many times a second.

details.didYouKnow: Many headsets draw the edges of each image in less detail than the centre, a trick called foveated rendering, because the lenses blur the edges anyway and your eyes rarely look there.
details.howItWorks: One chip holds the main processor cores, a graphics processor, an image processor for the cameras and AI hardware for hand tracking. Each frame it draws the scene twice, once from each eye's position, then bends the image to cancel out the distortion of the lenses. Just before the frame goes to the screen, it warps the image again using the very latest head position, which hides small delays.
keyNumbers: Draws roughly 9 million pixels per frame across both eyes
Typically 90 to 120 frames per second
Aims to keep motion-to-photon delay under about 20 milliseconds
details.madeOf: A silicon die made with transistors only a few nanometres across, packaged in plastic and often with the memory chips stacked or placed right beside it. Short connections save power and speed up data.

parts.name: Processor chip

parts.description: Accelerometer and gyroscope chip that measures every tilt and turn of your head, far more often than the cameras can look.

details.didYouKnow: Your inner ear is very sensitive to a mismatch between what you feel and what you see. A big part of why this sensor matters is simply that a delay of a few hundredths of a second can make people feel ill.
details.howItWorks: Cameras can only look at the room a few dozen times a second, which is far too slow on its own to keep the picture steady as your head turns. This chip measures rotation and acceleration perhaps a thousand times a second. The headset uses it to predict where your head will be when the next picture appears, then corrects the slow drift using what the cameras see.
keyNumbers: Often sampled around a thousand times a second
A few millimetres across
Combined with camera tracking to cancel drift
details.madeOf: Tiny silicon structures on microscopic springs, etched from a chip and sealed in a small package. Movement shifts them by a tiny distance, which is measured electrically.

parts.name: Motion sensors

parts.description: Metal fins that draw heat out of the processor so the fan can blow it out of vents in the top.

details.didYouKnow: A heat pipe can move heat many times better than a solid copper bar of the same size, because a liquid inside boils at the hot end and condenses at the cool end.
details.howItWorks: Heat flows from the processor into the heat sink through a thin layer of thermal paste or pad, which fills microscopic gaps between the two surfaces. The heat spreads along the metal and into its thin fins, which have a large surface area for air to carry heat away. Keeping the chip cool lets it run fast for longer and keeps the front of the headset comfortable against your face.
keyNumbers: Copper conducts heat roughly 1.7 times better than aluminium
Aluminium is roughly a third as dense as copper
Fins typically under 1 mm thick
details.madeOf: Aluminium or copper, sometimes with a flattened heat pipe or vapour chamber inside. Copper conducts heat better, while aluminium is lighter, and weight matters a lot on your head.

parts.name: Heat sink

parts.description: Small, quiet fan that pulls air through the visor and over the heat sink.

details.didYouKnow: Unlike most phones, many standalone headsets need a fan because they run their chips hard for long periods and cannot spread the heat into a hand holding them.
details.howItWorks: The fan draws cool air in through vents and pushes it across the heat sink's fins, then out of the top of the visor where the warm air rises away from your face. Its speed rises and falls with how hard the processor is working, so it stays nearly silent in menus and speeds up in demanding games. Without it, the headset would have to slow down sooner to avoid overheating.
keyNumbers: Typically only a few centimetres across
Usually spins thousands of times a minute
Power use typically well under 1 W
details.madeOf: Moulded plastic blades on a tiny brushless motor, usually with a fluid or sleeve bearing for quiet running. Plastic keeps the spinning parts light, which reduces noise and vibration.

parts.name: Cooling fan

parts.description: Lithium-ion battery along the bottom of the visor, good for roughly two hours of play.

details.didYouKnow: Lithium-ion cells age faster when kept fully charged and warm, so a headset left plugged in on a sunny windowsill wears its battery out quicker.
details.howItWorks: The battery powers everything through power-management chips on the logic board, which convert its voltage for the processor, displays and cameras. A protection circuit watches temperature, voltage and current, and cuts off charging if anything goes wrong. Placing heavy parts low and close to the face helps with balance, though many people add a rear battery pack partly as a counterweight.
keyNumbers: Around 5,000 mAh capacity
Roughly 2 to 2.5 hours of play
Typically charges fully in around 2 to 3 hours
details.madeOf: Lithium-ion cells with a graphite anode and a metal-oxide cathode, wrapped in a thin foil pouch or metal case. Lithium-ion stores a lot of energy for its weight, which matters on your head.

parts.name: Battery

parts.description: Fast LCD panel with roughly 2,000 by 2,200 pixels, one for each eye, showing that eye's view of the scene.

details.didYouKnow: Earlier headsets showed a faint grid between pixels, nicknamed the screen-door effect, because the lenses magnify the panel so much; denser panels have made it far less visible.
details.howItWorks: A bright backlight shines through a layer of liquid crystals that twist to let more or less light through each red, green or blue sub-pixel. To avoid blur when you turn your head, the backlight only flashes on briefly once each frame, a trick called low persistence. The image on the panel looks warped and squashed, because it is pre-distorted to cancel out the bending of the lens in front.
keyNumbers: Roughly 2,000 by 2,200 pixels
Typically 90 to 120 refreshes per second
Pixels typically change in a few milliseconds
details.madeOf: Glass sheets sandwiching liquid crystal, colour filters and transistors, over an LED backlight. Fast-switching liquid crystal formulas are used so pixels can change in a few milliseconds.

parts.name: Left display

parts.description: Folded 'pancake' lens that bounces light back and forth between polarising layers, so it can sit very close to the screen.

details.didYouKnow: Your eyes can resolve roughly 60 pixels per degree, so even sharp modern headsets still show less detail than the real world.
details.howItWorks: Light from the display passes through a half-silvered mirror, travels to a reflective polariser that bounces it back, returns to the mirror, and finally passes through on its way to your eye. Folding the light path like this lets the lens sit just a couple of centimetres from the screen while still making it look large and far away. The catch is that much of the light is lost on the way, so the displays must be very bright.
keyNumbers: Field of view about 110 degrees across
Lets through at most about a quarter of the display's light
Roughly 25 pixels per degree of view
details.madeOf: Several thin elements of optical plastic or glass, coated with a partial mirror, a quarter-wave plate and a reflective polarising film. Plastic is lighter, glass scratches less and stays more stable with heat.

parts.name: Left pancake lens

parts.description: Fast LCD panel with roughly 2,000 by 2,200 pixels, one for each eye, showing that eye's view of the scene.

details.didYouKnow: Using two pictures to fool the brain into seeing depth goes back to the stereoscope, invented in the 1830s, long before photography was common.
details.howItWorks: The right display shows the same scene as the left but from a viewpoint a few centimetres further right, and your brain merges the two into one 3D image. Both panels are refreshed in step with each other and with the processor, so neither eye sees a frame the other has not. The software also nudges the image to match your lens spacing so the centre of each picture lines up with each eye.
keyNumbers: About 4.5 million pixels each
Roughly 1,200 or more pixels per inch
Typically about 5 cm across
details.madeOf: A thin-film transistor LCD on glass, with a polarising film on each side and an LED backlight behind. LCDs are cheaper and brighter than OLEDs at this size, which helps make up for the light lost in pancake lenses.

parts.name: Right display

parts.description: Folded 'pancake' lens that bounces light back and forth between polarising layers, so it can sit very close to the screen.

details.didYouKnow: Because the focus distance is fixed, your eyes focus at the same distance even when a virtual object appears right in front of your nose, which is one reason close-up objects can feel tiring to look at.
details.howItWorks: The right lens matches the left exactly and moves with it when you turn the spacing wheel. Pancake lenses give a sharper image across more of the view than older ridged Fresnel lenses, so you can glance towards the edges without everything going blurry. The lens also makes your eyes focus as though the screen were a metre or two away rather than a few centimetres.
keyNumbers: Typically sits a couple of centimetres from the display
Focus set to appear about 1 to 2 m away
Clear area typically a few centimetres across
details.madeOf: Optical-grade plastic or glass with an anti-reflection coating on the outer surfaces. The coating cuts stray reflections, which would otherwise show up as glare or ghost images.

parts.name: Right pancake lens

parts.description: Two polished rods and a toothed rack: the lenses slide along the rods, and the wheel drives the rack to set their spacing.

details.didYouKnow: Some headsets skip mechanical adjustment and show a smaller picture through a wider sweet spot instead. It saves parts, but people far from the average eye spacing can notice blur toward the edges.
details.howItWorks: People's eyes are different distances apart, so each lens rides on two polished rods and can slide sideways. Turning the wheel under the visor drives a toothed rack, which moves the lenses apart or together by equal amounts. If the lenses sit out of line with your pupils, the picture looks blurred or strained, so this small mechanism has a big effect on comfort.
keyNumbers: Adult eye spacing is typically around 55 to 70 mm
Adjustment is usually a few steps or a smooth range of about 15 mm
details.madeOf: Polished steel rods for low friction, with moulded plastic or metal lens carriers and a small gear and rack.

parts.name: Lens rails

parts.description: Thumbwheel under the visor that slides the two lenses apart or together to match the distance between your eyes.

details.didYouKnow: The distance between your pupils, called interpupillary distance or IPD, usually differs between people by more than a centimetre, which is why one fixed setting cannot suit everyone.
details.howItWorks: Turning the wheel drives a small mechanism that moves the two lens and display assemblies apart or closer together by the same amount. When each lens is centred on each pupil, the image is sharpest and the 3D effect is correct. The headset reads the position of the mechanism and tells the software, which adjusts the images to match.
keyNumbers: Adjusts from roughly 58 to 71 mm
Average adult spacing about 63 mm
Usually continuous rather than set steps
details.madeOf: Moulded plastic with a ridged grip, driving metal or plastic gears and rails inside. Plastic gears are light and quiet and need no oil.

parts.name: Lens spacing wheel

parts.description: Plastic shell of the visor that everything mounts into, with vents for the fan and slots for the strap arms.

details.didYouKnow: The first head-mounted display, built in 1968, was so heavy it hung from the ceiling on a mechanical arm, earning the nickname the Sword of Damocles.
details.howItWorks: The housing holds the optics, electronics and battery in exact positions relative to each other, which matters because the tracking cameras must stay perfectly aligned with the displays. It forms channels for cooling air, keeps light from leaking into the lenses and gives the strap arms solid places to clip in. Its shape also shields the electronics from knocks.
keyNumbers: Whole headset weighs about 500 to 520 g
Visor roughly 18 to 19 cm wide
Typically a few centimetres deep thanks to pancake lenses
details.madeOf: Injection-moulded plastics such as polycarbonate or ABS, often reinforced inside with ribs or a metal frame. Plastic keeps weight down and can be moulded into complex shapes in one piece.

parts.name: Visor housing

parts.description: Soft, removable foam-and-fabric cushion that rests on your face and blocks out light from the room.

details.didYouKnow: Fitness apps made sweat-resistant, wipeable face cushions popular, because foam soaks up moisture during an intense workout.
details.howItWorks: The cushion spreads the headset's pressure over your forehead and cheeks and seals out room light that would otherwise reflect in the lenses. It usually clips on magnetically or with tabs, so it can be swapped for cleaning or for a different fit. A small proximity sensor just inside can tell when the headset is on your face and wake the displays.
keyNumbers: Foam typically a couple of centimetres thick
Carries a large share of the roughly 500 g headset
Glasses spacers usually add several millimetres of room
details.madeOf: Soft foam covered with fabric or wipe-clean synthetic leather. Foam moulds to the shape of your face, and wipeable covers are popular for shared or exercise use.

parts.name: Face cushion

parts.description: Rigid side arm that links the visor to the head strap and carries the left speaker past your ear.

details.didYouKnow: Many owners replace the stock strap with a rigid halo or rear battery strap, which moves weight from the face to the top and back of the head.
details.howItWorks: The left arm clips into the side of the visor and runs back to the fabric strap, holding the visor at a steady angle. A hinge where it meets the visor lets the front tilt up and down to find the clearest part of the lenses. The arm also routes wires from the logic board to the speaker it carries.
keyNumbers: Typically about 10 to 15 cm long
Weighs typically only a few tens of grams
Typically joins the visor at one hinge point
details.madeOf: Stiff plastic, sometimes with a glass-fibre filler, with a softer rubber or fabric coating where it touches your head. Stiffness stops the visor from bobbing when you move.

parts.name: Left strap arm

parts.description: Speaker in the strap arm that aims sound at your left ear without covering it, for directional 3D audio.

details.didYouKnow: Because the speakers do not cover your ears, people near you can hear what you are hearing, so headphones are still the choice for privacy.
details.howItWorks: A small driver pushes sound out of a grille aimed at your ear canal from just in front of your ear, without touching it. The headset makes sound seem to come from a particular place by changing the volume, timing and tone each ear hears, a technique called spatial audio. As you turn your head, the mix updates instantly, so a sound stays fixed to its spot in the virtual room.
keyNumbers: Driver typically only a couple of centimetres across
Sits roughly 1 to 2 cm from the ear
Covers roughly the range of human hearing, about 20 Hz to 20 kHz, though bass is weak
details.madeOf: A thin polymer diaphragm moved by a copper voice coil and a small neodymium magnet, in a moulded plastic chamber. The chamber's shape is tuned to boost the bass a driver this small would otherwise lack.

parts.name: Left speaker

parts.description: Rigid side arm that links the visor to the head strap and carries the right speaker past your ear.

details.didYouKnow: A front-heavy headset presses mostly on your cheeks and forehead, so balancing weight between front and back often matters more for comfort than reducing total weight.
details.howItWorks: The right arm mirrors the left, and the two together form a rigid frame that stops the visor twisting on your face. Strap tension is shared between the two arms so the headset sits evenly. On many headsets the arms can be unclipped completely so you can swap in a different strap.
keyNumbers: Typically about 10 to 15 cm long
Shares roughly half the strap's pull
Usually a few millimetres thick
details.madeOf: Moulded engineering plastic, chosen to be tough enough to survive being dropped or squashed in a bag. A metal pin or clip often forms the hinge where it meets the visor.

parts.name: Right strap arm

parts.description: Speaker in the strap arm that aims sound at your right ear without covering it, for directional 3D audio.

details.didYouKnow: Your brain can tell which side a sound came from using arrival-time differences of less than a thousandth of a second between your two ears.
details.howItWorks: The right speaker works with the left to place sounds anywhere around you, including behind and above. Software applies filters based on how your head and outer ears shape sound, which is how the brain tells front from back. A gunshot from your right arrives at your right ear slightly louder and sooner than your left, and the headset copies that.
keyNumbers: Arrival time difference between ears up to about 0.7 milliseconds
Typically a single full-range driver per side
Sits roughly 1 to 2 cm from the ear
details.madeOf: A tiny moving-coil driver with a fine mesh grille to keep out dust and sweat. Neodymium magnets give a strong push from a very small, light part.

parts.name: Right speaker

parts.description: Elastic fabric strap round the back of the head, adjusted with sliders to spread the headset's weight.

details.didYouKnow: A headset that feels light in your hand can feel heavy after an hour, because its weight sits several centimetres in front of your face and acts like a lever pulling your head forwards.
details.howItWorks: The strap goes round the back of your head, usually splitting into two parts to cradle the bulge at the back of the skull. Tightening the sliders pulls the visor against your face, and setting it snugly but not tightly keeps the image steady without pressing too hard. A good fit puts more of the weight on the back of your head and less on your cheeks.
keyNumbers: Headset weighs about 500 to 520 g in total
Strap weighs typically a few tens of grams
details.madeOf: Woven elastic fabric with plastic sliders and buckles. Fabric is light, cheap, washable and folds flat, though it gives less support than a rigid strap.
